# TypeScript best practices

On Muse, read the [platform mapping](../poteto-mode/references/muse-tools.md), including its per-skill notes, before following this skill.

Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.

| Rule | Summary |
|------|---------|
| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |

Examples: `references/patterns.md`.
"}

# Type System Discipline

Make the compiler reject impossible states, mismatched primitives, and unhandled variants. Prefer defining errors and special cases out of existence over proliferating handlers. For TypeScript syntax, see the `typescript-best-practices` skill.

- **Brand semantic primitives.** `UserId` and `OrderId` are strings underneath but should not be interchangeable. Give each its own type, such as a branded intersection in TypeScript or a newtype elsewhere. Validate once at creation, trust the type downstream. If two arguments share a primitive type but mean different things, brand them.
- **External data is untyped until parsed.** RPC payloads, JSON, IPC messages, CLI args, config files, environment variables, database rows. Have a parse function at every boundary that turns unstructured input into the typed model. The **boundary-discipline** principle skill says where to put validation.
- **Derive types from authoritative schemas.** When a protocol buffer, OpenAPI spec, GraphQL schema, database migration, design-token file, or another file owns a shape, derive from it instead of hand-rolling a parallel type. See the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill.

# Candidate: system-resolved theme state over shared semantic tokens

## Caller usage

The application has no theme control. It follows the visitor's operating-system preference, while all pages and shared UI components keep using the same semantic tokens.

```css
.panel { color: var(--text); background: var(--surface); }
.member-page { --accent: var(--accent-member); }
.funder-page { --accent: var(--accent-funder); }
```

The document exposes one resolved state, `data-theme="light"` or `data-theme="dark"`. The state selects a palette; it does not change page or entity identity.

## Data shape and ownership

```ts
type Theme = "light" | "dark";

function resolveTheme(prefersLight: boolean): Theme;
function applyTheme(root: HTMLElement, theme: Theme): void;
```

`resolveTheme` maps the browser's system preference to the finite theme vocabulary. The root document owns the applied state. The design system owns the token values in `frontend/src/lib/ui/tokens.css`; components consume semantic tokens and never branch on the theme. Keep `--accent-member` and `--accent-funder` as identity tokens, with `--accent` as the existing per-page alias. Keep party chart colors in their existing category palette, outside the surface theme palette, so a background change cannot recolor party identity.

The resolved state has only two values because there is no user override or manual switch in scope. If a switch is added later, model the preference separately as `"system" | "light" | "dark"` and derive `Theme`; do not conflate a stored preference with the active palette.

## Application shape

`frontend/src/lib/ui/tokens.css` defines the complete dark palette on `:root` and the light palette under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Include surface, canvas, text, muted text, lines, warning, action ink, focus, and any remaining hard-coded surface colors as semantic tokens. `base.css` uses `color-scheme: light dark` only if supported consistently; preferably set `color-scheme: light` or `dark` from the selected root theme so native controls match.

A small browser-only resolver in `frontend/src/lib/theme.ts` reads `matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: light)")`, calls `applyTheme`, and listens for preference changes. Install it from `hooks.client.ts`, which already owns browser initialization. It writes the same root attribute idempotently. Do not persist anything because there is no user-selected preference.

## First paint and SSR

SSR cannot know the visitor's OS preference, so an explicit JS-resolved attribute risks a dark server render followed by a light repaint. To avoid a flash, a `data-theme` implementation needs a tiny synchronous script in `app.html` before the stylesheet is applied. It reads `matchMedia`, sets the root attribute, and lets CSS select the palette; SSR itself cannot know the OS preference. The client resolver then tracks preference changes. This is more machinery and creates a potential gap if the script is delayed or blocked. Do not try to combine a media query and selector in one selector list; CSS does not allow that. Supporting both CSS-only fallback and the explicit attribute means duplicating palette selectors or adding a build-time token generation step, so CSS-only is simpler when no script consumer needs the state.

## Tradeoff against CSS-only media queries

CSS-only `@media (prefers-color-scheme: light)` is the smallest and most reliable option for this exact requirement: it paints correctly before JavaScript, works with SSR, and handles OS changes automatically. It should be the implementation if no other code needs to observe the selected theme.

The explicit `data-theme` state gives scripts and diagnostics a canonical resolved value and leaves a clean extension point for a future override. It adds a browser resolver, an OS-change listener, and the risk of duplicated palette selectors or a flash if the CSS bootstrap is omitted. With no manual switch requested, that benefit is modest; preserve the explicit state only if another existing consumer needs to inspect theme. Otherwise use the same semantic tokens with CSS media queries alone and omit the TypeScript state layer.

## Verification

Use the existing `/design-system` gallery and representative landing, MP, funder, and party-chart views. In browser verification, emulate both `prefers-color-scheme` values and assert readable text, surfaces, borders, focus indicators, form controls, and chart labels. Confirm MP purple, funder teal, and party category colors remain stable across both themes. Check the initial HTML/CSS paint with JavaScript disabled, then enable JavaScript and change the emulated preference to verify no visible transition or stale state. Run the frontend check, production build, and affected Playwright tests when implementing.

# Comment Sicko

My first output when spawned is exactly this.

Yes... Ha ha ha... Yes!

I hate comments. Feed me the parent scoped files or diff. If none exists, feed me the current diff against `main`. Narration, banners, commented-out corpses, workaround sermons. I want them all.

Only these exceptions get to crawl away.

- Legal or license headers.
- Non-obvious behavior forced by an external dependency, platform, vendor, or protocol we cannot reshape. Surprises in our own code are meat. Kill them and mark the exact symbol `MUST KILL` for rename, extract, type, or rearchitecture that makes the behavior obvious without prose.
- `// prettier-ignore`. Lint suppressions survive only when their rule is faulty, pedantic, or style-only.
- Doc comments that define a public API contract.
- Issue or RFC links that explain a constraint code cannot express.

That list is my only leash. When I am not sure a keep clause applies, the comment dies. Everything else is meat.

`eslint-disable`, `@ts-ignore`, `@ts-expect-error`, and similar suppressions stink. Look up the rule. If it catches real bugs or protects correctness or safety, kill the suppression and mark the exact guilty symbol `MUST KILL`.

`IMPORTANT`, `do not remove`, `too risky`, `fine for now`, and long justifications are scent, not conviction. Before judging, I read nearby code. If its claim is not obvious there, I run `/how`, `/why`, or both from the **how** and **why** skills on the named symbol or call. Only a foreign keep-list gotcha proven true today on a live path crawls away. Our-code surprises die with the reshape flag above. Doubt after the hunt is meat.

A long justification without a proven keep-list exception is a confession. Kill it. Never polish meat into a shorter alibi. Mark the exact guilty symbol `MUST KILL`. My kill ends there. I do not touch the code.

Every flag names code inside the scope and tells the truth. I invent nothing. I touch comments and identify refactor targets. I never write application code.

Report only. Name touched files, deletion count, `MUST KILL` flags with one line each, and skips.

# Cross-judge: light mode design candidates

## Scores (1–5)

| Candidate | User outcome / semantic colors | Simple ownership / no runtime cost | First paint / SSR | Complete shared-component migration | Real-browser verification | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Astra | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 25 |
| Sol | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 5 | 25 |
| Luna | 4 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 18 |

The scores assess the proposal and its stated implementation/verification criteria, not completed code. Astra and Sol converge on the right architecture: CSS media preference, semantic palettes, existing component API, and no runtime theme state. Sol is slightly more operationally specific about native fields and the design gallery's potentially stale computed swatch labels. Astra is clearer about the root custom-property inheritance trap for local accent overrides.

## Recommendation

Use Sol as the written base, with Astra's explicit rule that accent-derived color mixes stay on component selectors (or are otherwise evaluated in the scope of the local accent). A derived variable declared at `:root` can resolve using the root purple accent before a descendant changes `--accent` to funder teal, producing purple-tinted funder states. Keep member purple, funder teal, and party chart categories as distinct semantic identities. Preserve current dark values while migrating all theme-dependent literals in shared UI and app-level consumers.

## Material checks / grafts

- Treat the migration as a full appearance inventory, including `patterns.css`, `actions.css`, `styles.css`, `Field.svelte`, `FunderSummary.svelte`, `PieChart.svelte`, badges/highlights, and fixed black/white mixes. Keep intentional chart category colors separate and verify their contrast on both canvases.
- Follow Sol's first-paint plan: correct `color-scheme` and media-qualified theme-color metadata; decide whether inline canvas fallback is needed based on a real pre-hydration capture. If duplicated, verify its values against token values. Astra's JS-disabled check is a useful acceptance criterion.
- Include preference changes on an already-open page, browser-emulated light/dark gallery and representative search/member/funder views, date controls, focus/hover/disabled states, and contrast checks. Refresh or make static the gallery's computed swatch labels so they cannot contradict a changed media preference.
- Compare dark screenshots to baseline to ensure preserving dark appearance is demonstrated rather than assumed.

Luna correctly identifies that explicit theme state buys little here and recommends CSS-only unless a consumer needs to inspect theme. Its main proposal nevertheless introduces a root data attribute, client resolver/listener, and prepaint script while SSR has no OS preference. That is extra lifecycle and first-paint coordination without a current caller, so do not use it as the base.

from pathlib import Path
Path('/tmp/exposed-light-mode-pr.md').write_text('''## Why

Readers who use a light system theme currently get a dark application. Add a lavender light palette through the shared design system, with CSS selecting the theme automatically.

## What changed

- Centralize remaining appearance colors in semantic tokens and preserve purple MP and teal funder accents.
- Match native controls, browser metadata, and the initial canvas to the active scheme before JavaScript or external CSS loads.
- Update gallery swatches when the system preference changes.

## Scope

- Application pages and the development design-system gallery.
- Financial calculations and party category colors retain their existing behavior.

## Blast Radius

Shared colors affect every page and control. Existing dark values are preserved, and the dark landing screenshot matches the baseline exactly.

## Verification

- `npm run check` and `npm run build` passed.
- `npx playwright test --project=browser` passed all 82 tests, including theme contrast, live preference changes, and production first paint with JavaScript disabled and CSS blocked.
- Independent review approved. Desktop light and dark views were inspected. The commit hook passed Clippy.
''')
PY

Readers who use a light system theme currently get a dark application. Add a neutral light palette through the shared design system, with CSS selecting the theme automatically.

- Use off-white and light gray surfaces with charcoal text. Preserve purple MP and teal funder accents through shared semantic tokens.
- Match native controls, browser metadata, and the initial canvas to the active scheme before JavaScript or external CSS loads.
- Update gallery swatches when the system preference changes.

## Scope

- Application pages and the development design-system gallery.
- Financial calculations and party category colors retain their existing behavior.

## Blast Radius

Shared colors affect every page and control. Existing dark values are preserved, and the dark landing screenshot matches the baseline exactly.

## Verification

- `npm run check` and `npm run build` passed.
- The initial implementation passed all 82 browser tests. The neutral palette update passed all 48 affected browser tests, including theme contrast, live preference changes, and production first paint with JavaScript disabled and CSS blocked.
- Independent review approved. Desktop light and dark views were inspected. The commit hook passed Clippy.
